stem:
A 6-year-old boy of Greek background develops jaundice, dark urine and pallor 2 days after starting trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole for a urinary tract infection. He has mild tachycardia but no bleeding or rash, and his urine output is normal.

| Test | Result | Reference range |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Haemoglobin | 72 g/L | 115–155 |
| Reticulocytes | 9% | 0.5–2.5 |
| Platelets | 260 × 10⁹/L | 150–450 |
| Creatinine | 40 µmol/L | 25–60 |
| Direct antiglobulin test | Negative | Negative |
| Blood film | Blister cells and irregularly contracted cells; no schistocytes | No abnormal forms |

Which underlying disorder is most likely?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Drug-induced immune haemolysis usually gives a positive direct antiglobulin test; his is negative.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Correct. Acute haemolysis 2 days after an oxidant drug in a boy of Mediterranean background, with a negative antiglobulin test and blister and irregularly contracted cells, fits G6PD deficiency. The enzyme level can be falsely normal during the reticulocytosis, so repeat it later if needed.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Spherocytosis gives spherocytes on the film, often with splenomegaly and a family history; this film shows oxidant damage instead.

options.label: D
options.explanation: HUS needs thrombocytopenia, schistocytes and kidney injury; his platelets, film and creatinine are normal.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria causes intravascular haemolysis after an infection, with a positive antiglobulin test for complement; his test is negative and the trigger is a drug.

context: G6PD deficiency can cause acute oxidant-triggered haemolysis with jaundice, dark urine, reticulocytosis and bite cells. A normal enzyme test during haemolysis may need later repetition.
